assessment_summary: The statement claims that for every n >= 4, a self-complementary graph on n vertices exists. For a graph to be self-complementary, it must have the same number of edges as its complement, meaning it must contain exactly half of the edges of the complete graph K_n. The total number of edges in K_n is n(n-1)/2, so a self-complementary graph must have n(n-1)/4 edges. This requires n(n-1) to be a multiple of 4, which only occurs if n ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4). For n = 6, n(n-1)/4 = 30/4 = 7.5, which is not an integer. Thus, no self-complementary graph exists on 6 vertices.
counterexample: n = 6. A self-complementary graph on n vertices must have exactly n(n-1)/4 edges. For n = 6, n(n-1)/4 = 30/4 = 7.5 edges, which is impossible. Therefore, there is no self-complementary graph on 6 vertices.
